title: Constant-factor approximation for Densest k-Subgraph
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\) and every integer \(1\le k\le |V|, A(G,k)\) outputs a set \(S\subseteq V\) with |\(S|=k\) and |\(E(G[S])|\ge \operatorname{OPT}(G,k)/C\), where \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=\max _{T\subseteq V, |T|=k}|E(G[T])|\)?
definitions: G is explicitly represented by its vertices and edges, and k is supplied in binary as part of the input. \(G[S]\) contains all edges of G with both endpoints in S; loops and parallel edges are absent. The running time is polynomial in the full input length with a fixed exponent independent of k. The same finite C must work for all graphs, all graph sizes and all choices of k; it cannot increase with \(n=|V|\) or with k. The output must be a vertex set, not only an estimate of the optimum. When OPT=0, every k-set meets the requirement. Because all feasible sets have the same cardinality, maximizing edge count, average degree \(2|E(G[S])|/k\), or edges per selected vertex gives the same approximation objective. No promise of a clique, graph expansion, metric edge weights or a random input distribution is supplied. This card fixes deterministic algorithms; a randomized constant-factor guarantee would be major progress but has a distinct derandomization requirement. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Densest k-Subgraph is a basic test of how well algorithms can identify a concentrated combinatorial structure. Its unresolved approximation landscape influences many reductions and separates strong evidence of difficulty from the hardness consequences currently obtainable from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

importance.reason: A flagship approximation problem with a simple objective, a large algorithmic gap, strong conditional and relaxation barriers, and consequences for several other optimization problems.

progress.text: Bhaskara and coauthors obtain \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in polynomial time for each fixed \(\varepsilon\); the exact quarter-power endpoint has quasipolynomial running time in this work.
Bhaskara and coauthors prove polynomial integrality gaps for strong SDP hierarchies, establishing barriers for those relaxations.
Manurangsi proves almost-polynomial-ratio hardness under ETH, with perfect completeness; the revised April 2017 manuscript appears at STOC 2017.
Chuzhoy and coauthors publish a 2-CSP conjecture and conditional superconstant NP-hardness for DkS, together with reductions to related graph objectives.
Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar publish an exact continuous penalization and a nonconvex optimization method; no general constant-factor polynomial-time guarantee is established.
Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi give reductions to Densest At-Least-k-Subgraph and explicitly retain the missing NP-hardness of even 1.001 approximation for DkS.

status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The constant-factor algorithm is already ruled out assuming ETH, which remains unproved. The May 2026 primary source explicitly notes the absence of NP-hardness of approximation even at factor 1.001. This card asks about a deterministic constant-factor algorithm on all unweighted graphs, and preserves the distinction between conditional evidence and an unconditional resolution.

context_blocks.text: The task asks for a fixed-size collection of vertices containing as many internal interactions as possible. The cardinality restriction is what turns an otherwise tractable density objective into a central approximation problem. Without a prescribed size, maximizing edges per vertex can be solved in polynomial time. Allowing at least k vertices also changes which solutions compete: a large moderately dense region may be a valid answer even when no comparably useful k-vertex portion can be extracted.

Exact optimization contains CLIQUE: a graph has a k-clique precisely when \(\operatorname{OPT}(G,k)=k(k- 1)/2\). This observation alone gives almost no multiplicative approximation gap. A k-set missing only one possible edge is nearly optimal as k grows, even though it is not a clique. To rule out a constant-factor algorithm, a reduction must create a substantial separation between the best densities of its YES and NO instances, not merely a one-edge difference.

Bhaskara, Charikar, Chlamtac, Feige and Vijayaraghavan achieve \(O(n^{1/4+\varepsilon})\) approximation in \(n^{O}(1/\varepsilon )\) time for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Their method uses small tree patterns and a hierarchy of conditioned information to identify a dense region. The \(O(n^{1/4})\) phrase in the paper’s title needs care: attaining that endpoint in their analysis takes quasipolynomial \(n^{O}(\log  n)\) time. Neither rate is a constant approximation.

There is substantial evidence against the target. Manurangsi proves that ETH rules out even approximation within \(n^{1/(\log  \log  n)^{a}}\), for a universal constant \(a>0\). ETH asserts that 3SAT has no \(2^{o}(N)\)-time algorithm on N variables. This is a stronger assumption than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\); the result therefore already excludes every fixed constant under ETH, while leaving the weaker-assumption hardness problem unresolved. Its YES instances can contain a k-clique, a property called perfect completeness.

Semidefinite-programming lower bounds supply a different kind of evidence. Bhaskara, Charikar, Guruswami, Vijayaraghavan and Zhou construct polynomial integrality gaps for strong hierarchies of relaxations. A relaxation can assign a large fractional or vector-valued objective even when no genuine k-set has comparable density. Such a gap limits approximation guarantees obtained from that relaxation, but it is not a theorem excluding every polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm.

Chuzhoy, Dalirrooyfard, Grinberg and Tan propose a 2-CSP hardness conjecture that would imply NP-hardness of approximating Densest k-Subgraph within \(2^{(\log  n)^{\varepsilon}}\) for some \(\varepsilon >0\). Their paper also connects its approximability to graph partitioning, dense coloring and bounded-crossing subgraphs. Some connections use quasipolynomial reductions, so they should not be read as constant-factor polynomial-time equivalences. The conjectural premise remains a real part of the hardness claim.

Laekhanukit, Manurangsi and Trabelsi’s May 2026 paper still reports that no NP-hardness of approximation is known for Densest k-Subgraph even at factor 1.001. They show that the absence of any constant-factor DkS algorithm implies a \((3/2- \varepsilon )\) barrier for the at-least-k density problem. This transfers a hypothetical negative answer to a neighboring objective; the neighboring problem’s known 2-approximation does not answer this card.

An AAAI 2026 result by Liu, Liu, Ma and Konar gives an exact continuous penalization reformulation and an efficient nonconvex proximal-gradient method. Exactness concerns the relationship between optima of the formulations. It does not mean the method finds a global optimum, or even a fixed approximation ratio, on every graph in polynomial time. The distinction explains how useful practical progress can coexist with the unresolved worst-case guarantee.

sentences: Densest k-Subgraph asks which exactly k vertices of a graph contain the most internal edges.
The target is a polynomial-time algorithm whose edge count stays within one universal constant of optimum.
Fixing the number of vertices prevents using a larger, moderately dense region as a substitute.
Such a guarantee would clarify a central gap in approximation theory and influence several related network problems.
The saved review describes strong conditional hardness under ETH, while distinguishing this evidence from hardness based only on \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).
